claims.question: Why is skip and limit wrong for the bookings list, not just slow?
claims.claim: Skip and limit is wrong because while bookings are being created, a new booking shifts every later one down by a place.

sources.title: pagination-design.pdf / Problem
sources.text: The bookings list pages with skip and limit. Two things go wrong. It gets slower the deeper a client pages, because the database still walks past every skipped booking: page five hundred reads ten thousand bookings to return twenty. claims.question: Why does the URL shortener answer with a 302 rather than a 301?
claims.claim: If a 301 were used instead, browsers would remember it, and after the first visit the clicks would never arrive at the service.

sources.title: interview-notes.pdf / Document
sources.text: URL SHORTENER - MOCK INTERVIEW NOTES One hundred million new links a month, each read about a hundred times for every time one is written. Links never expire unless their owner deletes them. A seven character code drawn from a 62 character alphabet gives about 3.5 trillion codes, enough for centuries at this rate. POST /links with the long URL returns the short code. GET on the code answers with a 302 redirect rather than a 301, so that every click reaches the service and can be counted; a 301 is remembered by browsers, and after the first visit the clicks would never arrive. Each server takes a block of one million ids from a coordinator and hands them out in order, encoded in base 62. No two servers can produce the same code, so nothing has to be checked against the database before a link is created, and the coordinator is asked for a new block only once per million links. One table: the code, the long URL, the owner and the time it was created, with the code as the key. Most redirects are for a small set of popular links, so those are kept in memory on each server and the database only sees the long tail. WHAT I MISSED Abuse: nothing stops someone shortening a phishing link, and a shortener with no review is a gift to them. Analytics: counting clicks at a hundred reads per write needs its own pipeline rather than a database write on every redirect.

claims.question: What error does the API return when a cursor is reused with a different filter?

sources.title: pagination-design.pdf / Edge cases
sources.text: If the booking a cursor points at is deleted, paging still works: the cursor holds the start time and id themselves, not a reference to look up, so the next page simply begins after those values. A cursor is only valid for the filter it was made with. claims.question: What went wrong in my mock system design interview?
claims.claim: In the mock interview, Priya went straight into the database schema without saying how many reads there were for each write.

sources.title: learning-log.pdf / Document
sources.text: Week one. The practice API crashed twice this week and both times the cause was the same: an async route handler threw, nobody caught the rejected promise, and the process died with an unhandled rejection. Express 4 does not catch errors from async handlers on its own. I wrapped every handler in a small function that passes the error to next, and the crashes became ordinary error responses. What confused me was that the crash did not happen in development, because there the error was thrown before the first await. What I would do differently: read the error-handling page of the framework before writing twenty routes, not after. Week two. Read about idempotency before starting the webhook assignment and realised the old handler had been doing double work for months without anyone noticing, because the duplicates were rare enough to look like customer mistakes. The idea that finally made sense is that retries and idempotency are one design, not two: retrying something that is not safe to repeat turns a reliability feature into a correctness bug. I was confused about where the key should come from until I looked at what the provider sends. Week three. Mock system design interview with Priya: design a URL shortener. I went straight into the database schema and the hashing scheme and never said how many reads there were for each write, which turns out to be the question the whole design hangs on, since a shortener is read far more than it is written. Priya's feedback was to state my assumptions out loud in the first two minutes, numbers included, before drawing anything. I am going to open every practice question that way from now on. Week four. Load testing. I expected the CPU to be the limit and it was the connection pool, which I had never thought about as a thing with a size. The lesson I wrote down: measure before guessing, because my guess was confidently wrong. Week five.

claims.question: What would make me switch the orders service away from documents?
claims.claim: You would switch the orders service away from documents if the service itself started needing questions across items, such as stock reservation where every order line has to be checked against what is left.

sources.title: orders-schema.pdf / Document
sources.text: Both designs answer it in a few milliseconds once the customer id and the placed date are indexed together, and there was nothing to choose between them. The second query is total revenue per product per month, across two hundred thousand generated orders. Postgres answered it with a GROUP BY over order_items in 0.4 seconds. MongoDB needed an aggregation that unwinds every order's items before grouping them, and took 1.8 seconds. The gap is the cost of storing items inside orders: a question about items, rather than about orders, has to take every order apart first. Where each one hurts The document model hurts on reporting, as the second query shows, and on any question that cuts across orders. It also means a product renamed today keeps its old name on old orders. For this service that is correct rather than a flaw: an order is a record of what was bought, and a receipt should not change after the fact. The relational model hurts on the common path. Every order view is a three-table join, every new order is several inserts that must be wrapped together, and the schema has to change in a migration whenever a new kind of order detail appears. The orders service uses the document model. Orders are written once, read whole, and almost never queried by their items, which is the shape documents suit. The reporting cost is real, and the answer to it is not to compromise the service's own schema: a nightly export copies orders into Postgres, where the revenue reports run without touching the live database. The decision would flip if the service itself started needing questions across items - stock reservation, say, where every order line has to be checked against what is left.

claims.question: Why can't the webhook just record the event id first?
claims.claim: Recording the event id first does not help, because a crash after recording would charge the customer twice.

sources.title: queue-retries.pdf / 5 Open questions
sources.text: One case is not solved. If the handler charges the customer and then crashes before it records the event id, the redelivery will find no record and charge again. Recording the id first has the opposite failure: a crash after recording and before charging means the payment is never taken. Fixing it properly needs the charge and the record to succeed or fail together - a transaction, if both live in one database, or passing our own key to the ledger service so that it can refuse the duplicate itself.

claims.question: Why is it acceptable that renaming a product leaves old orders unchanged?
claims.claim: Renaming a product leaves old orders unchanged, because each order stores a snapshot of the product's name at purchase.

sources.title: orders-schema.pdf / Document
sources.text: Both designs answer it in a few milliseconds once the customer id and the placed date are indexed together, and there was nothing to choose between them. The second query is total revenue per product per month, across two hundred thousand generated orders. Postgres answered it with a GROUP BY over order_items in 0.4 seconds. MongoDB needed an aggregation that unwinds every order's items before grouping them, and took 1.8 seconds. The gap is the cost of storing items inside orders: a question about items, rather than about orders, has to take every order apart first. Where each one hurts The document model hurts on reporting, as the second query shows, and on any question that cuts across orders. It also means a product renamed today keeps its old name on old orders. For this service that is correct rather than a flaw: an order is a record of what was bought, and a receipt should not change after the fact. The relational model hurts on the common path. Every order view is a three-table join, every new order is several inserts that must be wrapped together, and the schema has to change in a migration whenever a new kind of order detail appears. The orders service uses the document model. Orders are written once, read whole, and almost never queried by their items, which is the shape documents suit. The reporting cost is real, and the answer to it is not to compromise the service's own schema: a nightly export copies orders into Postgres, where the revenue reports run without touching the live database. The decision would flip if the service itself started needing questions across items - stock reservation, say, where every order line has to be checked against what is left.

claims.question: Why does the URL shortener answer with a 302 rather than a 301?
claims.claim: The shortener answers with a 302 because a 301 would be cached by the database and the clicks would never be counted.

sources.title: interview-notes.pdf / Document
sources.text: URL SHORTENER - MOCK INTERVIEW NOTES One hundred million new links a month, each read about a hundred times for every time one is written. Links never expire unless their owner deletes them. A seven character code drawn from a 62 character alphabet gives about 3.5 trillion codes, enough for centuries at this rate. POST /links with the long URL returns the short code. GET on the code answers with a 302 redirect rather than a 301, so that every click reaches the service and can be counted; a 301 is remembered by browsers, and after the first visit the clicks would never arrive. Each server takes a block of one million ids from a coordinator and hands them out in order, encoded in base 62. No two servers can produce the same code, so nothing has to be checked against the database before a link is created, and the coordinator is asked for a new block only once per million links. One table: the code, the long URL, the owner and the time it was created, with the code as the key. Most redirects are for a small set of popular links, so those are kept in memory on each server and the database only sees the long tail. WHAT I MISSED Abuse: nothing stops someone shortening a phishing link, and a shortener with no review is a gift to them. Analytics: counting clicks at a hundred reads per write needs its own pipeline rather than a database write on every redirect.

claims.question: What failure case is still unsolved in my webhook design?
claims.claim: An unsolved case is when the handler charges the customer and then crashes before recording the event id, which causes a redelivery to find no record and charge again.

sources.title: queue-retries.pdf / 5 Open questions
sources.text: One case is not solved. If the handler charges the customer and then crashes before it records the event id, the redelivery will find no record and charge again. Recording the id first has the opposite failure: a crash after recording and before charging means the payment is never taken. Fixing it properly needs the charge and the record to succeed or fail together - a transaction, if both live in one database, or passing our own key to the ledger service so that it can refuse the duplicate itself.

sources.text: The third query is the one worth keeping: it is slow, it stays slow, and the honest fix is a second index on created date rather than pretending the existing one helps. claims.question: Why did the crash not happen in development?
claims.claim: The crash did not happen in development, because Express 4 catches errors from async handlers there.

sources.title: learning-log.pdf / Document
sources.text: Week one. The practice API crashed twice this week and both times the cause was the same: an async route handler threw, nobody caught the rejected promise, and the process died with an unhandled rejection. Express 4 does not catch errors from async handlers on its own. I wrapped every handler in a small function that passes the error to next, and the crashes became ordinary error responses. What confused me was that the crash did not happen in development, because there the error was thrown before the first await. What I would do differently: read the error-handling page of the framework before writing twenty routes, not after. Week two. Read about idempotency before starting the webhook assignment and realised the old handler had been doing double work for months without anyone noticing, because the duplicates were rare enough to look like customer mistakes. The idea that finally made sense is that retries and idempotency are one design, not two: retrying something that is not safe to repeat turns a reliability feature into a correctness bug. I was confused about where the key should come from until I looked at what the provider sends. Week three. Mock system design interview with Priya: design a URL shortener. I went straight into the database schema and the hashing scheme and never said how many reads there were for each write, which turns out to be the question the whole design hangs on, since a shortener is read far more than it is written. Priya's feedback was to state my assumptions out loud in the first two minutes, numbers included, before drawing anything. I am going to open every practice question that way from now on. Week four. Load testing. I expected the CPU to be the limit and it was the connection pool, which I had never thought about as a thing with a size. The lesson I wrote down: measure before guessing, because my guess was confidently wrong. Week five.

sources.text: The member lookup went from a collection scan over forty eight thousand documents to an index scan returning twelve. That is the only query where the index changed the plan shape rather than merely the cost. The feed query was already using the index on author, and adding the created date to it made the sort disappear from the plan. The report query on created date alone did not improve at all, because the compound index begins with author and the prefix rule means a query on the second field cannot use it.

answers.question: Why is skip and limit wrong for the bookings list, not just slow?
answers.answer: Skip and limit is wrong because while bookings are being created, a new booking shifts every later one down by a place [1]. As a result, a client paging through sees one booking twice and never sees another [1].

sources.title: pagination-design.pdf / Problem
sources.text: The bookings list pages with skip and limit. Two things go wrong. It gets slower the deeper a client pages, because the database still walks past every skipped booking: page five hundred reads ten thousand bookings to return twenty. And it is wrong while bookings are being created, because a new booking shifts every later one down by a place, so a client paging through sees one booking twice and never sees another.
